To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a thymol glycoside, thymol β-d-glucopyrano-side, was able to reduce Campylobacter concentrations in the crop of market age broiler chickens, but not in the ceca.

thymol-ß-d-glucopyrano-side, an orally administered, non-absorbed thymol derivative, reduced Campylobacter concentrations in the crop of market-age broilers by 10-fold, but did not affect Campylobacter levels in cecal contents.
thymol-ß-d-glucopyrano-side was more effective in reducing the recovery of Campylo-bacter from the crop contents of broiler chickens than thymol.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel, natural products to reduce carriage of food-borne pathogens in food animals.
the development and testing of novel antimicrobial compounds that are intended to be used in food animals as feed additives to reduce the prevalence of food-borne pathogens.
the development of novel, safe, and efficacious strategies to reduce the carriage and shedding of Campylobacters in food animals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the present studies indicate thymol- β-d-glucopyraoside is an effective antimicrobial agent in reducing the concentration of Campylobacte r jejuni in avian crop contents.
thymol- β-d-glucopyronaside has the potential to be an effective anti-Campylo-bacter agent when used as a preharvest feed additive.
thymol-ß-d-glucopyrano-side is more resistant to rapid absorption than free thylmol and is efficacious in reducing Campylobacter concentrations in the avian crop.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that thymol-ß-d-glucopyrannoside is more stable in vivo than thymol, and that the glycoside is effective at reducing Campylobacter concentrations in the crop of broiler chickens, but not in the cecum.
the use of a glycoside of thymol is more effective than thymol alone at reducing the numbers of Campylobacte in the avian crop.

the use of thymol as a natural preservative to reduce carriage of C.jejuni in poultry is promising, but the conjugation of thymol to a glucopyranoside did not yield a more effective anti-Campylocbacter compound in the avian gut.
The main takeaway from our work is that
thymol is not a suitable antimicrobial for in-feed use in chickens, as it was not retained in the crop or ceca.
the anti-Campylocbacter activity of thymol can be maintained by glycosylation and that this glycoside can be retained in the avian crop for at least 6 h after administration.
the efficacy of a feed additive in reducing Campylobacter carriage is dependent on the site(s) where the additive is active.
